Board Amendments

The printed Guide is a yearly snapshot; the board amends continuously. After each meeting, record anything rule-bearing here in one line — and record the quiet months too, so silence means “confirmed no change,” not “unknown.” This log is also next year’s Guide revision, built as it happens.

The Log

Nothing recorded yet.

Unreservable Booths

Booths no reservation can be taken on, available to vendors seeking a booth for Saturday or Sunday assignment. They are first handed out in the Thursday call-in round and stay in the pool for the in-person rounds after it. The Guide requires this list to be updated before the March round each year, once non-returning vendors are known.

The list is empty. The real 2026 list is a record the app has never been given — it lives with the Operations Manager, and is named on the Developer’s Records Needed desk. What is entered here is a working copy, not the source of truth.

Design questions that were settled in conversation, recorded so they stay settled. When a change is proposed that touches one of these, the principle is the starting position — it can be overturned, but only knowingly.

After a Major Change, Sweep These

A rename, a moved tool, or a rephrasing ripples further than the screen it happens on. This is the sweep list — each entry is a place stale wording has actually been found.

A screen is described in five places
Change what a tool is and five separate texts go stale, each written at a different time and none of them next to the others in the file. Walk all five, every time:
• The desk tile — the folder entry in MGR_FOLDERS, or the drawer’s fold-sub on the vendor desk.
• The screen’s own intro — the empty-note under its heading.
• The help dot — its entry in HELP_TEXTS, found by index and easy to mismatch. Read the title as well as the body: entry 45 sat under the wrong screen’s name for months.
• Plain Words — if the market has its own name for the thing.
• Anywhere else that names it — alerts, Records Needed, planned-tool explainers, other tools’ summaries.
Absence Patterns was rebuilt to watch deadlines rather than count absences, and for two builds the tile, the help dot and Plain Words all still described the leaderboard it had stopped being. A screen that contradicts its own description teaches people not to trust either.
Help dots
Every “?” whose screen changed. A rebuilt screen can orphan its help dot entirely — check the dot still exists, and that its text describes the screen as it now stands.
Explainers behind cones
Planned-tool text that names other tools, desks, or old vocabulary — including the footer state when a cone comes off.
Plain Words
If the market’s vocabulary moved, the ledger records it — old word kept in quotation marks as the bridge.
App Glossary
If the app’s own vocabulary moved — a desk renamed, a new kind of part invented — the glossary follows.
Crumbs and desk homes
A moved tool must crumb back to its new desk, and nothing should still say where it used to live.
Cross-references in other tools’ text
Summaries, alerts, tile descriptions and Records Needed entries that name the changed thing by its old name.
Screens shared between desks
A screen reachable from more than one desk carries every control it has to whoever opens it. Season-Long Booth Reservations sits on the vendor desk as well as the manager’s, and shipped Assign & Advance, Pass, and Release to vendors. Any control that writes the market’s records — rather than the person’s own — needs the manager-only class and a requireManager() check inside the function, because hiding a button does not withhold the power behind it. The vendor desk has now been swept; staff, volunteer and kiosk have not. See BF15. Two questions to ask of any card on a shared screen: does this person need it, and is it theirs to see? A card can pass the second and fail the first \u2014 that is how a manager’s ledger of booth holdings ended up on a vendor’s desk.
Correcting a seeded record
Changing a value in BOOTH_SEED, DEMO_VENDORS_SEED, REQUIREMENT_SEED or the Winter dates now reaches sheets that already exist — but only where nobody has edited that field. Adding a new collection to the seed means adding it to SEED_MERGE as well, or its records become permanent the first time they are written. And when a seed value changes for a record that may already be in the wild under the old value, name the old value in LEGACY_SEED_BIRTH so sheets written before the stamps existed can still be corrected. Watch the size of the birth keys: booths and vendors sit near 22,000 characters against a cell limit around 50,000.
Reconcilers correct, they do not invent
Code that repairs records on load may clear a value that cannot be true, but must never fill in a different one. reconcileBoothReservations used to turn an ineligible Saturday reservation into a Sunday-only booth, granting a vendor a holding they never won at any auction, silently, on every load. Clearing is honest; substituting is a fabrication that later reads as fact.
Map piece kinds
Placed pieces record only the kind’s key, and the pieces themselves live in the sheet, not in the build. Renaming or removing a kind orphans every piece already placed under the old key — so a kind’s key is permanent even when its label changes.
Beta Reset must not ship
Any build headed for real market use sets BETA_RESET_TOOLS to false. The reset desk rewrites records for every phone; it exists only to clean up after testing. A new storage key must also be added to BETA_RESET_KEYS as traffic or as configuration — a key in neither group is silently spared, and the screen’s three lists are drawn from that same table.
The handoff document
The next session inherits whatever the handoff says — it must describe the app as shipped, not as remembered.

What This Checks

Nearly every leak found in testing has belonged to one of four faults, and each one can be looked for by machine. Reports were being fixed one instance at a time while the rest of the class sat undisturbed — this walks the whole population instead. It cannot judge whether wording is good, only whether it is consistent, and it knows nothing of faults nobody has named yet.

What It Found

What the Guide Allows

A legitimate non-profit may, when space allows, use a market stall once during the season to hand out information and educate the public, after contacting the Organizational Manager. There is no application window and no deadline — the Guide sets none. What it does set are conditions:

• They may not sell anything, solicit donations, or accept donations.
• They may not be aggressive, or advertise their presence at market without approval.
• No soliciting or campaigning by political, religious, or other special interest groups is permitted at the market at all — by visitors or vendors.
• Non-political voter registration is the one named exception, with manager approval.

How This Works

The app fills an empty sheet with invented records so the market can be seen working before the real ones arrive. Every seeded field is stamped with the value it was born with. On each load, a field still matching its stamp is still the app’s own invention, so a build that corrects it delivers the correction. A field that no longer matches was changed by somebody — it keeps their value and loses its stamp, permanently. Fields the seed never set are never touched at all.

Ideas Worth Keeping

Name things after the market’s managers
Honor the people who have run the market over the years by putting their names on the things they cared for — a pavilion section, a bench, a gate, an annual award. The list of names lives with the office and the long memory of the members; the naming itself is a Board decision.

Records Needed

Nine records, each with a keeper. Any format works — a spreadsheet is enough. Together they might make one ask at a board meeting rather than nine.

Exceptions & Accommodations

Exception Request — the Guide calls this the “Special Needs Request”
Asks the Board to allow something the rules otherwise do not: a late fee, a shortfall against the attendance requirement, a Leave of Absence, a disability accommodation. It is a policy exception, whatever the reason. Submit at least one week before the December Board meeting.
Form not in project files — contact the Operations Manager directly

Product Applications

Value-Added Farm Products Application — the Guide calls these “Enhanced Agricultural Products”
For Ag vendors adding a made product (jam, cider, baked goods, etc.) built from what they grow. At least 75% of the finished product must be a farm-grown ingredient. Goes to the Ag Committee for jurying.

Add a Requirement

Some of the market’s oldest words describe something other than what actually happens. Where a word misleads, the app uses a plainer one and keeps the Guide’s word beside it. Where the word is fixed by the Guide or the Bylaws, the app keeps it and says here what it means.

Every value here is the rule as written, whether or not anyone has been enforcing it lately. When practice and paper disagree, this is the paper — the thing a manager or the Board can point to when a decision needs justifying. Each row names the document it comes from.

What Changed

Nothing has been changed from the Guide.

What This Screen Cannot Change

This screen changes numbers and dates. It cannot change how the market works.

Adding a booth request to Sunday, reordering who chooses first in a Booth Selection, adding a new approval step, changing who a rule applies to, or adding a screen — all of that is a change to the app itself and needs whoever maintains it. The same goes for anything not listed above: if a number is not on this screen, it is still written into the code.

Two things this screen does not do on its own. It does not rewrite a season that has already closed — a fee changed today does not restate last year’s invoices. And on a device with no shared storage, a change made here stays on that device.

New licences, permits and certificates do not belong here at all: add those in Vendor Requirements, which was built for exactly that.

Agenda & Tasks

What This Screen Can and Cannot Do

Committee membership is subject to Board approval, and chairs are appointed by the Board President (Bylaws, Article VI). This screen records those decisions so everyone can see them — it does not make them. Add people here after the Board has said yes, not before.

Time served on a committee counts toward a vendor’s work hour requirement. Hours are logged through Log Hours You Worked on the vendor’s own desk and signed off by the Market Manager — the committee chair keeps the meeting tally and passes it on, as the Food Committee guidelines describe.

A chair posting jobs directly is waiting on one record. The Guide raises no objection: committee service earns hours, and the only condition it sets is that “all other work hour assignments are subject to prior approval by the Market Managers.” So a chair could post a job to everyone or hand one to a particular vendor, with the manager signing it off — exactly the round trip logged hours now make. What is missing is knowing who chairs what. Until the rosters arrive the app cannot tell a chair from any other vendor, so the tool has nobody to belong to. The manager can already assign a task to one vendor from Work Hours Tasks.

Post a Task

Only they will see it. Work hours are not transferable, so an assigned task cannot be handed to somebody else.
